slides.title: Password Attack Indicators
slides.teach: Treat these as observable clues. On the exam, be ready to infer the most likely attack from the pattern of indicators.

slides.title: Spraying
slides.raw:
Spraying
Unusual access patterns
Simultaneous login attempts
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Password spraying tries one or a small number of common passwords against many accounts. It is designed to avoid lockout thresholds that would trigger if many guesses hit one account.
course.why: Large organizations often have some users with weak/common passwords.
course.example: An attacker tries “Welcome2026!” against 2,000 usernames, then waits before trying another password.
course.exam: One/few passwords → many users = spraying. Stolen username/password pairs reused elsewhere = credential stuffing.

breakdown.explanation: This concerns who or what can reach a resource and what actions are permitted once access is granted.

course.learn: A brute-force attack systematically tries many possible credentials, keys, or values until one works. It trades time and computing power for certainty.
course.why: Weak or short secrets make exhaustive guessing practical.
course.example: An attacker tries every four-digit PIN from 0000 through 9999.
course.exam: Brute force = exhaustive guessing. Password spraying uses a small number of common passwords across many accounts; dictionary attacks use likely words/passwords.

course.learn: A dictionary attack tries a curated list of likely passwords, words, patterns, and common variations instead of every mathematically possible value.
course.why: Human-chosen passwords are predictable, so likely guesses can be far more efficient than pure brute force.
course.example: A cracking tool tries common passwords, names, seasons, and substitutions from a wordlist against stolen hashes.
course.exam: Wordlist/likely passwords = dictionary attack; exhaustive all combinations = brute force.

slides.title: General Password Attack Mitigation Methods
slides.raw:
General Password Attack Mitigation
Methods
Strong Password Policies
Account Lockout Policies
Rate Limiting
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
Monitoring and Alerts
slides.teach: These are defensive actions. Learn what each one reduces and when it is the best response to a scenario.
defs: Multi-Factor Authentication: requires factors from more than one authentication category.

course.learn: Password-attack defenses combine strong password policy with rate limiting, lockout/throttling, MFA, secure password hashing, monitoring, and detection of breached credentials.
course.why: No single password rule stops every online and offline attack path.
course.example: A login system limits attempts per account and IP, requires MFA, and alerts on password spraying patterns.
course.exam: Rate limiting/lockout address online guessing; salting/key stretching protect stored hashes; MFA reduces the value of a stolen password.
